interactions.label: The pelvic ring has three articulations. In a young adult, why does a pubic rami

params.question: The pelvic ring has three articulations. In a young adult, why does a pubic rami fracture almost always have a corresponding injury at the posterior ring?

answers.text: Because the anterior pelvis absorbs more force than the posterior pelvis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The posterior ring, not the anterior, bears the majority of axial load. The reason for a second injury lies in the biomechanics of the ring itself.

answers.text: Because the pelvic ring is a rigid structure, so displacement at one point requires a second disruption elsewhere

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. A rigid ring cannot deform at a single point without yielding at a second. This is why an isolated anterior fracture on X-ray should prompt careful evaluation of the posterior ring on CT.

answers.text: Because the presacral venous plexus connects the anterior and posterior rings vascularly

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The presacral venous plexus is a major source of bleeding in pelvic fractures, but it does not explain why a second bony or ligamentous disruption must exist. The explanation is mechanical, not vascular.

answers.text: Because the sacroiliac joints are inherently hypermobile in young adults

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The sacroiliac joints are tightly bound by strong ligaments in young adults. In fact, it is the elderly pelvis, with weaker bone, that may sustain isolated ramus fractures without a second break.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the rigid-ring concept. A ring that breaks at one point can only displace if it also breaks or gives way at a second point. In a young adult's strong pelvis, an anterior fracture almost always has a posterior partner.
Exactly right. The rigid-ring principle is fundamental: always look for the second break, especially at the posterior ring, which determines stability and bleeding risk.

interactions.label: Preserved voluntary anal contraction alone is sufficient to classify a spinal co

params.question: Preserved voluntary anal contraction alone is sufficient to classify a spinal cord injury as incomplete on the ASIA Impairment Scale.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This statement is actually true. The concept of sacral sparing means that even one preserved function at the S4–S5 level reclassifies the injury from complete to incomplete. This distinction is critical because incomplete injuries have a significantly better prognosis. That is why S4–S5 must always be examined meticulously.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct. Sacral sparing means that even a single preserved S4–S5 function — voluntary anal contraction, perianal sensation, or deep anal pressure — changes the classification from ASIA A (complete) to incomplete, which carries a dramatically better prognosis for neurological recovery.

interactions.label: A trauma team is applying a pelvic binder on a haemodynamically unstable patient

params.question: A trauma team is applying a pelvic binder on a haemodynamically unstable patient with an open-book pelvic fracture. At which anatomical level should the binder be centred?

answers.text: At the level of the iliac crests

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This is the most common error. The iliac crests are too high and do not compress the pelvic ring effectively. The binder must sit at the greater trochanters to reduce pelvic volume.

answers.text: At the level of the greater trochanters

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Placing the binder at the greater trochanters compresses the pelvic ring and reduces its volume, which is most effective for counteracting the displacement in open-book injuries.

answers.text: At the level of the anterior superior iliac spines

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The ASIS level is still too high for optimal ring compression. The binder needs to sit lower, at the greater trochanters, to effectively close the displaced pelvic ring.

answers.text: At the level of the pubic symphysis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The pubic symphysis is too low and too anterior. A binder placed here would not adequately compress the posterior ring where the bleeding originates.

overallFeedback.feedback: The pelvic binder must be applied at the level of the greater trochanters, not the iliac crests or any other landmark. This is one of the most commonly tested and most commonly misapplied steps in pelvic trauma management.
Well done. Correct binder placement at the greater trochanters is a life-saving skill. It reduces pelvic volume and helps tamponade venous bleeding from the presacral plexus.

interactions.label: Open pelvic fractures carry a mortality rate of 30 to 50 per cent. What combinat

params.question: Open pelvic fractures carry a mortality rate of 30 to 50 per cent. What combination of factors is primarily responsible for this high lethality?

answers.text: Bilateral sacroiliac disruption combined with acetabular involvement

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While these patterns can coexist, the defining danger of open fractures is not the fracture pattern itself but the communication with contaminated spaces.

answers.text: Massive haemorrhage combined with faecal or urinary contamination leading to pelvic sepsis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The wound communicates with the perineum, vagina, or rectum, allowing bacteria to enter the fracture site. This contamination, on top of massive bleeding, drives pelvic sepsis and multiorgan failure.

answers.text: Arterial injury from the internal iliac artery, which is impossible to control with a binder

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While arterial injury can occur, most pelvic bleeding is venous. More importantly, it is the contamination through the open wound that distinguishes these injuries and drives the excess mortality.

answers.text: Neurological injury from sacral plexus damage, leading to autonomic instability

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Nerve injuries do occur and affect bowel and bladder function, but they are not the primary cause of the high mortality. The lethal combination is haemorrhage plus contamination.

overallFeedback.feedback: The key to understanding open pelvic fracture lethality is the dual hit: massive haemorrhage combined with contamination through a wound communicating with the perineum, vagina, or rectum. This combination leads to pelvic sepsis and multiorgan failure.

Exactly. Open pelvic fractures are a surgical emergency because the wound connects the fracture to contaminated spaces. Early recognition of a perineal, vaginal, or rectal wound is the house officer's most important contribution.

params.question: In a patient with a pelvic fracture and ongoing haemodynamic instability, why can a negative FAST scan be misleading?

answers.text: FAST has poor sensitivity for detecting solid organ injuries in trauma

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: FAST can detect free fluid from solid organ injury reasonably well. The issue in pelvic trauma is the location of the bleeding, not the sensitivity of the scan for intraperitoneal fluid.

answers.text: Pelvic fracture haemorrhage is primarily retroperitoneal, which FAST cannot detect

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. FAST detects free intraperitoneal fluid, but pelvic fracture bleeding collects in the retroperitoneal space. A negative FAST therefore does not rule out life-threatening pelvic haemorrhage.

answers.text: FAST requires intravenous contrast to visualise pelvic vasculature

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: FAST is an ultrasound-based assessment that does not use contrast. It detects free fluid in the peritoneal cavity, pericardium, and pleural space — but not retroperitoneal blood.

answers.text: Haemodynamic instability causes bowel gas artefacts that obscure pelvic images

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Bowel gas can reduce image quality, but the fundamental limitation is that FAST surveys the peritoneal cavity while pelvic fracture blood accumulates retroperitoneally.

overallFeedback.feedback: The key point is anatomical: pelvic fracture haemorrhage accumulates in the retroperitoneal space, which lies behind the peritoneum. FAST only surveys the peritoneal cavity, so it misses this bleeding entirely. A negative FAST in a haemodynamically unstable pelvic fracture patient should never be reassuring.

Exactly right. This is a classic pitfall in trauma management. Never let a negative FAST reassure you in a patient with a pelvic fracture and haemodynamic instability — the bleeding is retroperitoneal and invisible to FAST.
